content: Adverse reactions associated with the use of cephalexin include the following: 1. Gastrointestinal Reactions: Pseudomembranous colitis may develop during or after antibacterial treatment. Nausea and vomiting have been reported, though these are rare occurrences. Diarrhea is the most commonly reported side effect, but it is very rarely severe enough to necessitate discontinuation of therapy. Other gastrointestinal symptoms such as dyspepsia, gastritis, and abdominal pain have also been observed. Rarely, transient hepatitis and cholestatic jaundice have been reported, similar to reactions seen with some penicillins and other cephalosporins. 2. Hypersensitivity Reactions: Allergic reactions such as rash, urticaria (hives), and angioedema have been observed. Rarely, more severe hypersensitivity reactions, including erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported. These reactions typically resolve upon discontinuation of the drug, though supportive therapy may be required in some cases. Anaphylaxis, a severe and potentially life-threatening allergic reaction, has also been reported. Other hypersensitivity-related symptoms include genital and anal pruritus, genital moniliasis (yeast infection), vaginitis, and vaginal discharge. 3. Neurological and Psychological Reactions: Dizziness, fatigue, headache, agitation, confusion, and hallucinations have been reported. 4. Musculoskeletal Reactions: Arthralgia (joint pain), arthritis, and other joint disorders have been observed. 5. Renal Reactions: Reversible interstitial nephritis has been reported rarely. 6. Hematological Reactions: Eosinophilia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and hemolytic anemia have been reported. Slight elevations in liver enzymes such as AST (aspartate aminotransferase) and ALT (alanine aminotransferase) have also been noted. 7. Additional Adverse Reactions and Laboratory Abnormalities: Fever, colitis, aplastic anemia, hemorrhage, renal dysfunction, and toxic nephropathy have been reported with cephalosporin-class antibiotics. Seizures have been associated with cephalosporins, particularly in patients with renal impairment when the dosage was not appropriately adjusted. If seizures occur, the drug should be discontinued, and anticonvulsant therapy may be administered if clinically indicated. 8. Altered Laboratory Tests: Prolonged prothrombin time, increased blood urea nitrogen (BUN), elevated creatinine, elevated alkaline phosphatase, elevated bilirubin, elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), pancytopenia, leukopenia, and agranulocytosis have been reported. These adverse reactions and laboratory abnormalities should be carefully monitored during cephalexin therapy, and appropriate clinical measures should be taken if they occur.
